title: How to Pay Yourself From a US LLC as a Non-Resident in 2026
content:
# How to Pay Yourself From a US LLC as a Non-Resident in 2026

Getting money out of your US LLC and into your hands is the part most guides skip. Here is exactly how it works, what the IRS expects, and the fastest, cheapest methods available in 2026.

---

## The Basics: How a Single-Member LLC Is Taxed

For most non-residents, a US LLC is a **disregarded entity** or treated as a foreign partnership. This matters because it determines how you pay yourself.

- **Single-member LLC (disregarded):** All profit flows directly to you. There is no "salary." You take owner's draws.
- **Multi-member LLC:** Treated as a partnership. Profit is allocated per the operating agreement.
- **LLC taxed as S-Corp:** Requires a reasonable salary paid through payroll. This is rare for non-residents and comes with significant compliance overhead.

> **Note:** Non-residents cannot elect S-Corp status for their US LLC. If someone is pitching you that structure, get a second opinion before proceeding.

---

## Owner's Draws: The Standard Method

An owner's draw is simply a transfer of funds from your LLC's business bank account to your personal account. There is no payroll involved, no withholding, and no W-2.

**How it works in practice:**

1. Your LLC collects revenue into its US business bank account.
2. You transfer funds to yourself via wire transfer, ACH, or a multi-currency platform like Wise.
3. You record the draw in your bookkeeping software as an owner's draw (not an expense).

**Critical point:** Owner's draws are not tax-deductible business expenses. You are moving profit, not paying a salary. Do not categorize these as expenses in your books.

---

## What the IRS Actually Requires From Non-Residents

This is where most people get it wrong.

### FBAR and FinCEN Reporting

FBAR obligations apply to US persons who have a financial interest in or signatory authority over **foreign (non-US) bank accounts** that exceed $10,000 in aggregate value at any point during the year. Your US business bank account does not trigger FBAR. However, if you also hold funds in non-US bank accounts and meet the threshold, that is a separate filing obligation entirely.

Your home country may also have its own equivalent foreign account reporting rules. Do not assume you are in the clear without checking both sides.

### Form 5472 and Form 1120 (Disregarded Entity)

If you are a non-resident operating a single-member LLC, the IRS requires you to file **Form 5472** alongside a pro forma **Form 1120**. This applies when there are reportable transactions between you (the foreign owner) and the LLC, which includes every owner's draw you take.

- Filing deadline: 15th day of the 4th month after the tax year ends (typically April 15).
- Penalty for non-filing: $25,000 per form, per year. This is not a drill.

> **Note:** Form 5472 is not optional even if your LLC made zero profit. If you had any transactions with your LLC, file it.

### EIN Requirement

You need an EIN to open a US bank account and to file your annual forms. No EIN means no compliant operation. See our [LLC Guide](/llc-guide) for step-by-step instructions.

---

## The Fastest Ways to Transfer Funds Internationally in 2026

| Method | Speed | Cost | Best For |
|---|---|---|---|
| Wise (Business) | 1 to 2 days | 0.4% to 1.5% | Most currencies, low fees |
| Wire Transfer (SWIFT) | 2 to 5 days | $15 to $45 per transfer | Large amounts |
| ACH (US only) | 1 to 3 days | Usually free | US personal accounts |
| Payoneer | 1 to 3 days | 2% or flat fee | Freelancers, marketplaces |
| Mercury + Wise combo | 1 to 2 days | Very low | Most popular among nomads |

**The setup most non-residents use in 2026:** Mercury for the business account, Wise for international transfers. Mercury has no monthly fees and integrates directly with Wise for cheap, fast international payouts.

---

## How Often Should You Pay Yourself?

There is no IRS rule on frequency for owner's draws. Monthly is common because it is easy to track. Quarterly also works well if your revenue is irregular.

**What matters more than frequency:**

- Keep business and personal finances completely separate.
- Document every draw in your bookkeeping records.
- Do not use the LLC account to pay personal expenses directly. Draw first, then spend.

---

## Tax Obligations in Your Home Country

The US does not withhold tax on owner's draws taken by non-residents from a disregarded LLC (assuming the LLC has no US-source income). However, your home country will almost certainly tax this income.

You need to understand:

- Whether your country has a tax treaty with the US.
- How your country classifies LLC income (some treat it as corporate income, others as pass-through).
- Whether you need to declare US LLC income on a local tax return.

This is not something to guess. Speak to a local tax professional who understands US LLC structures.

---

## Get This Right From Day One

One missed Form 5472 can cost you $25,000. One misclassified owner's draw can create an audit trail that unravels your books. These are not edge cases; they happen to real business owners every year.
